chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ali ibn al-Hakam from 'Ulay ibn Razin from Muhammad ibn Muslim from one of them (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about a man who married a woman and looked at her head and part of her body: may he marry her daughter? He said: No, if he saw from her what is forbidden for others to see, then it is not permissible for him to marry her daughter.

3- From him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ibn Mahbub from Khalid ibn Jarir from Abu al-Rabi' who said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) was asked about a man who married a woman and stayed with her for days, unable to consummate the marriage, except that he had seen from her what is forbidden for others to see, then he divorced her: is it permissible for him to marry her daughter?
He said: Is it permissible for him, when he has seen from her mother what he saw?
4- Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Fadala from Aban from Muhammad ibn Muslim from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) like it.

Therefore, the ruling in these narrations is a type of dislike (karahah) rather than prohibition (haram), because the one that necessitates prohibition is the first narration, because it is consistent with the apparent meaning of the Book. Allah, the Exalted, said: 'And your stepdaughters who are in your households from your wives with whom you have consummated the marriage; but if you have not consummated the marriage, there is no blame upon you [to marry them].'

key_terms.كَرَاهِيَة: Dislike (a legal status between permissible and forbidden)

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible for a man to marry his wife's daughter if he has seen her private parts but not consummated the marriage?
ai.summary: This hadith clarifies the juristic distinction between *karahah* (dislike) and *haram* (prohibition) regarding a man marrying his stepdaughter after viewing her private parts without consummation. While the first narration suggests prohibition based on the apparent meaning of the Quranic verse, the scholarly consensus in *Al-Istibsar* leans toward dislike, as the explicit Quranic condition for absolute prohibition is actual consummation (*dakhala*). This reflects the Shia principle of reconciling textual evidence with practical legal rulings, prioritizing the specific condition of consummation for the stricter ruling.
